 Higher education: Throw it away and start over
 By Tess Gleason , Dept. Opinion Editor 
 / 
 6 hours ago 
 View Story Comments 
 0 
 Like This Story 
 Share on Facebook 
 Share on X 
 Email this Story 
 Print this Story 
 Graphic Tess Gleason 
 This December, I’ll be the first of my family to graduate from college. Come May, I’ll walk the commencement stage, and in exchange for years of dedication, I’ll receive a college degree that will give me an edge in the job market and copious amounts of money — at least, that’s what society has promised me.  
 Meanwhile, President Donald Trump is defunding certain degrees his administration says aren’t providing students positive returns , and dismantling the federal student loan process as we know it. After the long decade Trump has been in my life, we can actually agree on something: parts of higher education are broken.  
 I’m not calling to defund liberal arts degrees and vocational professions. Like so many others, I’d like to watch a musical, go to therapy, and get my hair trimmed, especially by people who are properly trained to do so. That work keeps the world turning. Trump might not be completely wrong to point out that people with these degrees and certifications should make more money than those who don’t in the same profession, but he loses me by attacking the field itself rather than the cost of these programs or low wages.  
 The truth is that higher education has become way too expensive. Saddling graduates with debt they cannot afford once they enter a far-from-perfect job market is nothing new. But for some reason, college administrators (ahem) and politicians fail to resolve the injustices of higher education. As a first-generation college student attending a four-year private institution, I’ve seen and felt these challenges firsthand, and I cannot let them be ignored.  
 Issues start before stepping on campus  
 Picture this: You’re 17 and entering your senior year in high school. Your secondary school years are almost behind you, and soon you will be able to go after your dreams, because you should know what those are by now. These dreams, though, come at a cost, whether that’s financially or emotionally.  
 If you want to continue schooling, you must choose a degree you might not love, but that will allegedly earn you enough money to pay off the debt to earn it. Or you can go after your passion and, well, still accumulate student debt alongside nearly 43 million American student borrowers .  
 Then you must choose between a private or public four-year institution. Don’t have the money? Don’t worry, you can get a loan or put it on credit. In fact, go ahead and borrow money for everything. The average American has over $6,000 in credit card debt , so why shouldn’t you?   
 For most college students, this is a reality. The average student starts college at 18 , fresh out of high school, and most feeling societal pressure to enroll, as 86% of students surveyed by Inside Higher Ed in 2021 echoed these sentiments. In 2025, another Inside Higher Ed survey found that 27% of students said they fully understood what their tuition entailed, allowing them to budget properly, while 47% said they understood most but not all expenses. Considering that one in six Americans turns to loans to afford their education, contributing to $1.6 trillion in federal student loan debt reported by Congress in 2025 , we can clearly see how detrimental college unaffordability is. If accumulating debt is a slippery slope, then college education is Mount Everest.  
 But the problems with higher education start way before decision day, and arise during the application stage. 
 Legacy admissions & affordability 
 Oh, how I love the smell of nepotism and intergenerational wealth in the morning!  
 We’ve all heard of nepo babies, but did you know that nepotism can sneak its way into college admissions? You see it when applications ask whether a family member attended the college you’re applying to. These nepos are called legacy students, and at Ivy League schools — the epitome of collegiate success — they are four times more likely to be admitted than non-legacy applicants with identical test scores and grades, according to The New York Times . For first-generation college students, the disadvantage is obvious: You don’t have parents who went to college, so you won’t have the upper hand.  
 According to a 2022 study published in Sage Journals , legacy students are less likely to apply for financial aid and are more likely to come from affluent parents. In contrast, lower-income and first-generation students have historically relied more heavily on student loans and federal Pell Grants. As a National Association of Student Financial Aid study reported , these students are also less likely to rely on their parents for college financing and more likely to work to afford their education.  
 Legacy acceptance rates devalue the work of students trying to get their foot in the door and undermine the meritocracy America loves to preach about . What’s the point of being told your hard work will lead to success if a student with connections gets in instead of you? One would think politicians would try to tackle these disparities, and while you’d be kind of right, it depends on who has the advantage.  
 Politicians have gone after affirmative action, which aims to help marginalized groups that have been historically barred from higher education, arguing it violates the Fourteenth Amendment and undervalues individual merit. Regardless of whether you’re for or against affirmative action, the Supreme Court’s decision to ban race-conscious admissions in 2023 but not legacy admissions raises questions about who is allowed admission perks. Newsflash, it’s not those who need it most. 
 If only we had equal access to schools with better financial aid or tuition-free programs, then students wouldn’t have to rely on subsidy programs and go into debt.   
 It’s also a culture issue  
 Many studies report that college leads to poor sleep, mental health, and social lives among college students. We live in a world where that’s not an excuse. You must get in, get the funding, maintain the grades, get the internship, stay active on campus, and hold a job, all while getting out of there quickly because remember, you cannot afford it.  
 For first-generation and low-income people , these challenges are even more intense, as these students are more likely to have family and job commitments that take away from their schooling, social lives, and sleep schedules. A study from Georgetown University showed that working wasn’t a choice for these students, unlike their higher-income counterparts, who can work in jobs related to their majors. These students suffer academically as a consequence of trying to scrape by.  
 Look, I don’t hate higher education. I’ve learned a lot over the last three years here and experienced things many people in my hometown never will. But I’ve also dealt with my fair share of financial disasters, felt unsupported by Emerson College as a first-generation student, and felt backed into a corner when it came to financing my degree that only continues to increase in cost. To say I never felt the disadvantages I came into college with because of my socioeconomic position would be a lie, and I’m only just one small example.  
 While writing this, I found that Trump and I surprisingly have more in common than I thought. He’s also a first-gen student who likes to flaunt their Bachelor of Science degree. He’s obsessed with inflation, who owes him money, and, at least, seemingly cares about accessible education . But his plan to defund liberal arts and vocational certifications will affect the populations that already struggle to attain them, not because those fields are failing, but because the education systems fail those students.
